figures.caption: Figure 6: Per-dataset identity-guard fallback rate for the headline cross-block run of TabICLv2Retouche on TabArena-Lite. Each marker is one dataset, positioned by its number of rows (horizontal, log scale) and number of features (vertical, log scale). The color encodes the fraction of the 8 AutoGluon bag-folds on which the guard routed back to the unmodified TabICLv2 base, restricted to the single configuration that minimizes the held-out AutoGluon bag-fold validation error per dataset. Marker shape encodes problem type (circle: binary, square: multiclass, triangle: regression). Datasets at the extremes (fallback rate ≥ 0.75 or ≤ 0.05) are annotated.

Table 3: Full TabArena-Lite leaderboard for the headline cross-block run of TabICLv2-Retouche (Section 4.2). Ranked by Elo. Best per column in bold, second in italic. Train/predict times are per 1,000 samples.
Table 2: Hyperparameter search space for TabICLv2-Retouche. Defaults match the first of the 11 configurations evaluated in the headline cross-block run (Section 4.2).
Figure 4: Quality vs. compute trade-off on TabArena-Lite: improvability vs. training time (a) and improvability vs. inference time (b). Lower-left is better; markers denote leaderboard methods.

Figure 5: Critical-difference diagram (Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc, α = 0.05) over per-task ranks on TabArena-Lite, covering the headline TabICLv2-Retouche (cross) (T+E) run and every non-AutoGluon TabArena-Lite leaderboard method at its strongest protocol (24 entries total). Mean rank is on the horizontal axis (lower is better); horizontal bars connect methods whose pairwise rank difference is not statistically significant.

Figure 8: Pairwise win rates (%) among TabICLv2-Retouche variants (T+E) and the unmodified TabICLv2 (D) on TabArena-Lite. Cell (i, j) reports the percentage of datasets on which row method i outperforms column method j.

Table 1: Simplified TabArena-Lite leaderboard. TabICLv2-Retouche’s T and T+E variants use a 20× smaller per-dataset HPO budget than every tuned peer (10 random configurations vs. TabArena’s standard 200). Time columns are wall-clock per 1K samples. Bold rows mark TabICLv2-Retouche variants. Italic row marks the unmodified TabICLv2.

Figure 3: Quality vs. compute trade-off on TabArena-Lite: Elo vs. training time (a) and Elo vs. inference time (b). Upper-left is better; markers denote leaderboard methods. On the training-time axis (a), TabICLv2-Retouche (T+E) is the highest-Elo point on the Pareto frontier and dominates every other tuned-and-ensembled peer. On the inference-time axis (b), TabICLv2-Retouche (T+E) is the highest-Elo point on the frontier; TabICLv2-Retouche (T) lies on the same frontier as a loweroverhead variant.

Figure 2: Overview of TFM-Retouche. A preprocessed input x is passed through a gated residual adapter gϕ(x) = (1−α)⊙ x+α⊙ δ(x) before entering a frozen TFM. Only the adapter parameters ϕ are trained end-to-end through the frozen backbone fθ. After training, an identity guard falls back to the unmodified TFM when adaptation does not improve held-out validation performance.

Table 4: Mean rank on the TALENT classification subset (Accuracy, 170 datasets with at most 10 classes). Methods shipped with the TALENT toolbox are re-ranked over this dataset universe; their own coverage may be a subset, in which case the column n reflects that subset. Best per column in bold.

Figure 9: Pairwise win rates (%) for the four iso-backbone adaptation paradigms and the unmodified base on the TabArena-Lite classification subset (36 datasets, two datasets excluded for baseline OOM).

Figure 7: Magnitudes of the 15 largest off-diagonal entries of |H| for the first bag-member of TabICLv2-Retouche (T) on taiwanese_bankruptcy_prediction (TabArena-Lite ID 363706), sorted with the largest at the top. Pairs whose two ratios both appear as separate regressors in a named bankruptcy-prediction study [Altman, 1968, Shumway, 2001, Chava and Jarrow, 2004, Ohlson, 1980] are coloured green; the remaining pairs are grey.
